title: Academic CV for PhD Applications: Structure and an Example
content:
An academic CV should help a reader find evidence of your preparation quickly. Prioritise education, relevant projects, research experience and skills you can demonstrate; label publications and work in progress accurately.

This guide explains exactly how to structure an academic CV for PhD applications, what to include, what to leave out, and what a strong sample looks like.

  • Research question: Evaluated [specific question] using [method].
  • My contribution: Collected [type of data], implemented [tools], compared [baseline].
  • Evidence: Report, code repository or presentation link, where shareable.
  • Outcome: Describe the actual result, including limitations, without invented percentages.

Sample Research Project Entry (Illustrative)

Do not invent awards, metrics, publications or impressive-looking supervisors. Any sample CV below is illustrative only and must not be presented as a real candidate’s history.

A PhD CV is a factual record, not a personal advertisement. For many new applicants, one to three well-organised pages may be enough; follow an institution’s instructions if it specifies a length. Research experience, degree projects, methods, and your own contribution should be easy to find.

What a Strong Early-Career Academic CV Should Do

Academic CV vs Professional Resume

FeatureAcademic CVProfessional Resume
Length2-6 pages (grows with experience)1-2 pages
FocusResearch, teaching, publications, conferencesWork experience and skills
StyleChronological, comprehensiveConcise, targeted to the job
PhotosUsually omittedSometimes included
Personal detailsMinimal (name, contact, ORCID)Varies by country

For a PhD application, you are writing an academic CV. Do not try to compress it into one page — the admissions committee wants to see the full picture of your academic life.

The Standard Academic CV Structure

Follow this order. It is the format expected by admissions committees at almost every university worldwide.

1. Header (Name and Contact Information)

  • Full name (as it appears on your passport)
  • Email address (use a professional one, not a nickname from years ago)
  • Phone number (with country code)
  • Address (city and country are enough)
  • ORCID iD (if you have one — this is your permanent academic identifier)
  • LinkedIn or Google Scholar profile (optional but helpful)

Do not include your date of birth, marital status, nationality, or a photo. These are not expected in most countries and can be seen as unprofessional.

2. Education

List your degrees in reverse chronological order (most recent first). For each one, include:

  • Degree name and subject
  • Institution name and location
  • Dates of study
  • Grade or classification (e.g. First-Class Honours, GPA 3.8/4.0, 85%)
  • Relevant coursework or thesis title (especially if the thesis is relevant to your proposed PhD)

If you are currently studying, write "Expected completion: [Month Year]".

3. Research Experience

This is the most important section of a PhD application CV. List every research project you have worked on, including:

  • Title of the project
  • Supervisor's name and institution
  • Duration
  • Your role and specific contributions
  • Methods used, results, and outputs (publications, presentations, code)

Be specific. "Worked on a machine learning project" tells the reader nothing. "Developed a reinforcement learning agent in PyTorch to control a simulated robotic arm, improving task completion by 15% over the baseline" tells them exactly what you can do.

4. Publications and Conference Presentations

List publications in a consistent citation format (APA, MLA, or IEEE — choose one and stick to it). Include:

  • Journal articles (peer-reviewed)
  • Conference papers and presentations
  • Book chapters
  • Preprints (e.g. arXiv, bioRxiv)
  • Posters

If you have no publications, do not worry — leave the section out or state that you have presentations in preparation. Never list a paper that does not exist.

5. Teaching Experience

Include any teaching, tutoring, or mentoring you have done. This matters more for some PhD programmes (especially in the humanities) than others. Include:

  • Teaching assistant roles
  • Tutoring (paid or volunteer)
  • Guest lectures
  • Workshop leading
  • Mentoring undergraduate or high-school students

6. Awards, Grants, and Scholarships

List any academic awards you have received. Include:

  • Scholarships and fellowships
  • Prize for best dissertation or best student
  • Travel grants for conferences
  • Research grants, however small

Include the value if it is impressive, and always include the year.

7. Skills and Technical Competencies

List the technical skills relevant to your research:

  • Programming languages (Python, R, C++, MATLAB, etc.)
  • Software (LaTeX, MATLAB, STATA, SPSS, RStudio, Jupyter)
  • Laboratory techniques (PCR, microscopy, spectroscopy, etc.)
  • Languages (with proficiency level)

Only list skills you can actually use. If an interviewer asks you to explain your work in MATLAB and you cannot, you will be caught out.

8. Professional Memberships

If you are a member of a professional body or academic society, list it here. Examples include:

  • IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers)
  • ACM (Association for Computing Machinery)
  • APS (American Physical Society)
  • Royal Society of Chemistry
  • British Computer Society

9. References

Include two or three academic referees, usually your thesis supervisor and one or two other professors who know your work. Provide:

  • Full name
  • Position and institution
  • Email address
  • Relationship to you

Always ask your referees' permission before listing them.

What to Leave Out

  • Photo: Not expected in most countries (some European countries accept it, but omit it for international applications).
  • Date of birth, marital status, nationality: Not relevant and can invite bias.
  • High school education: Once you have a university degree, high school is no longer relevant.
  • Irrelevant work experience: A summer job in a café does not belong on an academic CV unless it is your only work experience.
  • Hobbies: Unless directly relevant to your research or teaching, leave them off.

Formatting Tips

  • Font: Use a clean, readable serif or sans-serif font (Times New Roman, Garamond, Calibri, or Arial).
  • Size: 11 or 12 pt for body text, 14 to 16 pt for your name.
  • Margins: 1 inch (2.5 cm) all around.
  • Spacing: Single or 1.15 line spacing within entries; add a blank line between entries.
  • Consistency: Same date format, same punctuation, same capitalization throughout.
  • PDF: Always save as PDF to preserve formatting.
  • File name: Use something like "FirstName_LastName_CV.pdf". Never "cv_final_v2.pdf".
  • Listing skills you do not have: Interviewers will test you. Only list what you can defend.
  • Inconsistent formatting: Different date formats, mixed fonts, uneven spacing — all signal carelessness.
  • Vague descriptions: "Worked on research project" tells the reader nothing. Be specific.
  • Too short or too long: A first-year student's CV should be 2 pages. A postdoc's can be 6. If yours is 1 page with only a Bachelor's and no research, it looks thin.
  • Typos: Proofread, then get someone else to proofread. A single typo can undermine an otherwise strong application.
  • Not tailoring the CV: A CV sent to a robotics lab should emphasise robotics research. A CV sent to a biology lab should emphasise biology.

Before you submit

Your academic CV is a record of everything you have done as a researcher. Start building it early — even as an undergraduate — and update it every time you finish a project, receive an award, or present at a conference.

When you apply for a PhD, remember that the committee is looking for evidence that you can do independent research. Every entry in your CV should support that claim.

Start your PhD search on NextApply, filter by your field, and read the lab's recent publications before you apply. A tailored CV is always stronger than a generic one.

Always use the official admissions, funding or immigration page as the final authority before applying. NextApply is an opportunity discovery platform, not the admissions office.

A project entry should show your own contribution

An illustrative CV entry could read: “Final-year project: [question]. Implemented [method], compared it with [baseline] and documented limitations in [report or repository].” Replace each placeholder with accurate information. If the project was collaborative, state which parts you completed. Keep submitted papers, accepted papers and work in progress in separate, clearly labelled categories. A technical skill is more credible beside an example of its use than in a long list of software names. Remove any result, metric or qualification that you cannot substantiate.

Relevant listings and guides on NextApply

To see how these questions apply to a real listing, review EPSRC CDT in Robotics and AI for Net Zero (RAINZ) PhD Programme. Compare its stated requirements with your own preparation and check the official source before applying.

You can also browse RAINZ CDT on NextApply and the doctoral training programmes category. Listings and recruitment windows can change.
